message: Use to collect predictable clichés, recurring events, or likely behaviors and mark them off as they occur.
relational_pattern: A supposedly spontaneous situation is exposed as a repeatable grid of familiar patterns.
example_context: Before the town hall, employees make squares for 'circle back,' 'synergy,' and 'we hear you,' then check them during the call.
near_miss_context: The events are novel, unrelated, and impossible to anticipate; a bingo card needs recognizable repetition.

name: dj khaled suffering from success meme
message: Use when having so many successes that the advantages become overwhelming
relational_pattern: Excessive success leads to a burden of advantages
example_context: Your popular event sells out so quickly that you spend all day answering requests for extra seats; respond with this mock complaint.
near_miss_context: A preventable failure creates extra work; the burden did not arise from excessive achievement.

name: Congratulations you are being rescued please do not resist
message: Use when an authority imposes unwanted 'help' while insisting the recipient should be grateful.
relational_pattern: Coercion is rebranded as rescue, leaving the beneficiary no right to refuse.
example_context: IT remotely replaces everyone's preferred setup with a mandatory tool and announces the improvement using this line.
near_miss_context: A friend offers assistance, accepts 'no,' and leaves the choice with you; voluntary support is not forced rescue.

name: Peter Parker's Glasses
message: Use to contrast a mistaken first impression with the clearer—and often surprising—reality revealed on closer inspection.
relational_pattern: Removing a perceptual filter changes what the same subject appears to be.
example_context: The role looks like a promotion until you read that it doubles the workload without raising pay; label the blurry and clear views.
near_miss_context: Two unrelated options are being compared rather than one thing being reinterpreted; the glasses sequence implies corrected perception.

name: Uncanny Pingu
message: Use when something familiar is altered just enough to become eerie, wrong, or deeply uncomfortable.
relational_pattern: Near-normal appearance produces more unease than an openly monstrous one.
example_context: A company recreates your usual login page with subtly different wording and spacing, and the team calls it uncanny.
near_miss_context: The page openly displays a clear error message; obvious failure lacks the unsettling almost-normal quality.

name: Black guy confused
message: Use when someone is baffled by illogical information
relational_pattern: Open disbelief at illogical statements
example_context: A coworker says the deadline is flexible but also that missing Friday is unacceptable, and you answer with this baffled look.
near_miss_context: The statement is coherent but uses a term you have not learned; asking for a definition is different from spotting broken logic.

name: I have failed you
message: Use when expressing sincere guilt after letting someone down
relational_pattern: Guilt arises from a specific failure to fulfill a responsibility
example_context: You promised to save your friend a seat and forgot, then send this dramatic apology when they arrive.
near_miss_context: A minor preference was never promised and nobody relied on you; solemn guilt would invent a serious obligation.

name: Inhaling Seagull
message: Use when someone takes one brief breath before unleashing a sudden loud complaint, demand, or outburst.
relational_pattern: A tiny pause serves as the intake for an immediately explosive reaction.
example_context: A friend sees that the group ordered pineapple pizza again, and you send the inhale panel before their inevitable rant.
near_miss_context: They calmly explain their preference after thinking for several minutes; measured discussion is not the seagull's abrupt scream.

name: Cool Cat Stroll
message: Use when someone walks away from a success, comeback, or bold act with effortless confidence.
relational_pattern: A victorious moment ends in an unhurried exit that assumes everyone noticed.
example_context: After solving the office mystery with one search query, your coworker posts the cat stroll and signs off.
near_miss_context: A person leaves apologetically after their attempt fails; the swaggering victory walk would reverse the mood.

name: Talking to Brick Wall
message: Use when repeatedly explaining to someone who refuses to listen
relational_pattern: Persistent explanation without acknowledgment
example_context: After explaining three times that the event is cancelled, your friend asks where to buy tickets, so you post this.
near_miss_context: The listener summarizes your point and asks a relevant follow-up; active engagement is not a brick wall.

name: Car turning
message: Use when someone abruptly abandons the sensible path to pursue a much more tempting option.
relational_pattern: A last-second swerve reveals which desire overrules the original plan.
example_context: You intend to save your evening for chores, then a friend messages 'board games,' so you label the exit ramp accordingly.
near_miss_context: A driver changes routes because the road is closed; a necessary detour is not temptation defeating discipline.

name: Buff Doge vs Crying Cheems
message: Use when contrasting a strong past with a weaker present
relational_pattern: Past strength versus current vulnerability
example_context: Label the muscular dog 'our old password policy: 30 characters' and the crying dog 'today: please add one number.'
near_miss_context: The compared eras perform equally well under similar conditions, so strength-versus-decline would be false nostalgia.

name: give me
message: Use to demand or eagerly reach for something desirable with immediate, almost grasping urgency.
relational_pattern: Want overwhelms patience, turning a request into an outstretched claim.
example_context: A coworker reveals an unused vacation day can carry over, and you reply 'give me' before they finish explaining.
near_miss_context: You decline an offer because you do not want the item; the reaching demand would communicate the opposite.

name: I choose you!
message: Use when selecting one person, object, tool, or option from a larger set for the task ahead.
relational_pattern: A chooser singles out the candidate they expect to deploy.
example_context: The team needs someone to present the demo, and your manager tags you with 'I choose you.'
near_miss_context: The whole group is invited equally and nobody is singled out; the Pokémon selection grammar does not apply.

name: FLOODING THUMBS UP
message: Use when someone signals that everything is fine while the situation visibly deteriorates around them.
relational_pattern: A reassuring gesture clashes with an emergency that is already impossible to ignore.
example_context: The release dashboard turns red across every service, and the on-call engineer sends this thumbs-up to the team chat.
near_miss_context: A small issue is contained and the status report accurately says it is stable; the irony requires worsening conditions.

name: Lean forward in your chair
message: Use when casual attention suddenly becomes serious interest because the stakes or quality just increased.
relational_pattern: A relaxed observer shifts into focused engagement at a decisive moment.
example_context: A routine demo reveals a feature your team desperately needs, and you post that you are leaning forward now.
near_miss_context: You have been intensely involved from the beginning; there is no change from passive viewing to focus.

name: Expanding brain 3 panels
message: Use when ranking ideas from ordinary to absurdly advanced
relational_pattern: Ideas escalate from practical to increasingly unrealistic
example_context: Rank solving a late task by working, automating it, and finally claiming deadlines are a social construct.
near_miss_context: The options have no ascending logic or comic claim to enlightenment; random ordering weakens the format.

name: Tired dad at computer
message: Use when someone has been working on a computer for hours without breaks
relational_pattern: Exhaustion from prolonged computer work and endless digital tasks
example_context: After spending the night fixing a relative's printer remotely, you send this as your final status update.
near_miss_context: You have just opened the laptop after a restful break; the accumulated digital exhaustion is missing.

name: So No Head
message: Use when denial of an expected reward or favor prompts a comically abrupt, disproportionate tantrum.
relational_pattern: Disappointment escalates instantly into destructive rejection and departure.
example_context: Your friend learns the café is out of their favorite pastry and jokingly responds 'so no croissant?' before leaving the chat.
near_miss_context: A scholarship applicant receives serious bad news and handles it thoughtfully; the slapstick tantrum would trivialize the loss.

name: When X just right
message: Use when a detail reaches exactly the preferred balance
relational_pattern: Deep satisfaction when a detail reaches exactly the preferred balance
example_context: The group finally finds a meeting time that inconveniences nobody, and you share this satisfied reaction.
near_miss_context: The compromise still excludes two essential people; functional but flawed is not 'just right.'

name: Robotnik Pressing Red Button
message: Use when committing to a dramatic or destructive action with one decisive press
relational_pattern: Committing to a dramatic or destructive action with one decisive press
example_context: After weeks of restraint, the moderator finally bans the obvious troll and posts this decisive button press.
near_miss_context: The choice remains under review and nobody has committed; the template signals the action has been taken.

name: See You Again
message: Use when marking an emotional goodbye, reunion, or promise to remember someone after a meaningful period apart.
relational_pattern: Separation carries affection forward: people acknowledge a bond that persists despite distance or departure.
example_context: A longtime teammate leaves for another country after the final project, and the group posts this beneath their farewell photos.
near_miss_context: Avoid for a routine goodbye before tomorrow's meeting; the format implies meaningful distance, memory, or reunion.

name: Imma Keep It Real With You Chief
message: Use when giving a blunt negative assessment without softening it
relational_pattern: Giving a blunt negative assessment without softening it
example_context: A friend asks whether their twelve-slide dating-app bio is charming, and you preface your honest rejection with this.
near_miss_context: They asked for encouragement before a stressful event, not an evaluation; blunt negativity would serve no useful purpose.

name: You recieve I recieve
message: Use when laying out a two-sided exchange where each party gets a specific benefit
relational_pattern: Laying out a two-sided exchange where each party gets a specific benefit
example_context: Propose: 'You receive my meeting notes; I receive your test data' using each side of the trade.
near_miss_context: One person gives everything while the other offers nothing; that is exploitation, not a two-benefit exchange.

name: angry chihuahua happy chihuahua
message: Use when contrasting an aggressive outward reaction with a delighted inner feeling, or vice versa
relational_pattern: Contrasting an aggressive outward reaction with a delighted inner feeling, or vice versa
example_context: You complain that a meeting was cancelled while secretly delighted to regain the hour, so label the outer and inner dogs.
near_miss_context: Your outward reaction accurately matches your private feeling; the two-state contrast has nothing to reveal.

name: It's a trap
message: Use when recognizing that an attractive offer or easy route conceals danger
relational_pattern: Recognizing that an attractive offer or easy route conceals danger
example_context: A free trial asks for a credit card and makes cancellation impossible to find, so your friend warns you with Admiral Ackbar.
near_miss_context: The offer has clear terms, no lock-in, and a trusted provider; attractiveness alone does not make it a trap.

name: A Wizard Is Never Late
message: Use when reframing lateness or delay as deliberate perfect timing
relational_pattern: Reframing lateness or delay as deliberate perfect timing
example_context: You enter the group call ten minutes late and claim you arrived precisely when you meant to, quoting Gandalf.
near_miss_context: Your delay caused harm and requires a sincere apology; whimsical reframing should not replace accountability.

name: Aliens Guy
message: Use when using aliens or another wild theory as the explanation for unrelated evidence
relational_pattern: Using aliens or another wild theory as the explanation for unrelated evidence
example_context: Nobody knows why the office lights flicker every Friday, so someone skips troubleshooting and proposes aliens.
near_miss_context: The electrician identifies a loose connection with direct evidence; a wild theory is no longer needed.

name: spongebob panic inside
message: Use when appearing calm externally while experiencing frantic internal panic
relational_pattern: Appearing calm externally while experiencing frantic internal panic
example_context: You calmly tell the client the demo is loading while privately messaging the team that production is down.
near_miss_context: Your anxiety is visible to everyone and you openly ask for help; there is no calm exterior to contrast.

name: skinner pathetic
message: Use when dismissing a weak effort or boast with concise contempt
relational_pattern: Dismissing a weak effort or boast with concise contempt
example_context: A rival boasts about answering two emails before lunch, and your friend replies with Skinner's contemptuous 'pathetic.'
near_miss_context: A beginner proudly reaches a meaningful first milestone; dismissing growth would be cruelty rather than comic one-upmanship.

name: Mr T Pity The Fool
message: Use when mocking sympathy for someone whose foolish choice created the problem
relational_pattern: Mocking sympathy for someone whose foolish choice created the problem
example_context: Your friend ignores five weather warnings, gets soaked, and you say you pity the fool who left the umbrella home.
near_miss_context: Someone is harmed by circumstances they could not foresee or control; blaming foolishness would be unfair.

name: Is this a bird?
message: Use when someone confidently applies the wrong category or buzzword to something they barely understand.
relational_pattern: A superficial resemblance becomes an absurdly incorrect classification.
example_context: A manager sees any chart with an upward line and asks, 'Is this growth?' using the butterfly label.
near_miss_context: A student tentatively asks an expert to identify an unfamiliar specimen; honest uncertainty is not confident misclassification.

name: Calling the police
message: Use when treating an annoying, absurd, or suspicious act as serious enough to report
relational_pattern: Treating an annoying, absurd, or suspicious act as serious enough to report
example_context: A housemate puts ketchup on an expensive steak, and you jokingly reach for the phone as if reporting a crime.
near_miss_context: The behavior poses real immediate danger; contact actual emergency services rather than communicate through a reaction meme.

name: What the hell is this?
message: Use when shock and confusion upon encountering an inexplicable result
relational_pattern: Shock and confusion upon encountering an inexplicable result
example_context: The supposedly final design arrives with six overlapping logos, and the team responds with this bewildered inspection.
near_miss_context: The result differs from your taste but follows the agreed requirements; dislike alone is not incomprehensibility.

name: Leo Oscars Meme
message: Use to celebrate someone finally receiving recognition that was famously delayed or repeatedly missed.
relational_pattern: A long sequence of near-wins ends with the overdue prize at last.
example_context: After years of doing invisible work, a colleague finally wins the company award and the team posts this.
near_miss_context: A newcomer wins on their first attempt without any history of near misses; the long-awaited subtext is absent.

name: Some of you may die
message: Use when a leader casually accepts harm to others for their own objective
relational_pattern: A leader casually accepts harm to others for their own objective
example_context: A manager volunteers the entire team for weekend work while keeping their own plans, prompting the Farquaad quote.
near_miss_context: A leader accepts the same risk, seeks consent, and minimizes harm; shared sacrifice is not callous expendability.

name: Spongebob chicken
message: Use to taunt someone for backing away from a harmless challenge or failing to act after boasting.
relational_pattern: Retreat is reframed as cowardice by an opponent trying to provoke participation.
example_context: A friend loudly claims they can handle spicy food, then refuses the mildest wing, so the table sends this chicken reaction.
near_miss_context: Someone declines a genuinely dangerous dare; respecting a safety boundary is not cowardice.

name: Honey wake up
message: Use when a new installment, update, meme, leak, or oddly specific recurring event has just appeared and must be seen immediately.
relational_pattern: Enthusiasm for fresh content overrides sleep and ordinary timing.
example_context: A niche podcast unexpectedly releases a bonus episode at midnight, and you message your fellow fan with this format.
near_miss_context: The information can wait and the sleeping person has asked not to be disturbed; urgency is neither shared nor playful.

name: spongebob worship
message: Use to express comically excessive devotion to a person, product, idea, or small favor.
relational_pattern: Admiration is inflated into full ceremonial reverence.
example_context: A coworker brings the exact cable that saves the demo, and the team labels them as the object of worship.
near_miss_context: You give proportionate, sincere thanks for substantial help; ordinary appreciation does not need exaggerated adoration.

name: newspaper
message: Use to turn an event, opinion, or bit of gossip into a bold public headline.
relational_pattern: Private information is framed as front-page news worthy of mass attention.
example_context: Your usually punctual friend arrives five minutes late, and the group mock-announces the event in giant newspaper type.
near_miss_context: You are quietly sharing sensitive information with one trusted person; headline treatment would violate the intended privacy.

name: Ain't Nobody Got Time For That
message: Use when rejecting a tedious, unnecessary, or time-consuming demand
relational_pattern: You decline a request that wastes your time
example_context: Someone proposes a daily two-hour status call, and the team answers that nobody has time for it.
near_miss_context: The task is brief, necessary, and prevents a larger failure; inconvenience alone does not make it pointless.

name: Steve Harvey Laughing Serious
message: Use when laughter stops instantly after a new detail makes the subject serious, personal, or threatening.
relational_pattern: Amusement flips to concern once the joke's hidden implication lands.
example_context: You laugh at a story about forgotten anniversaries until your partner asks today's date, then send this two-stage reaction.
near_miss_context: The conversation stays light and everyone keeps laughing; there is no sobering turn for the second panel.

name: The Rock Explaining
message: Use when earnestly explaining an obvious point at excessive length
relational_pattern: You over-explain a simple concept with unnecessary detail
example_context: You ask where lunch is, and your colleague begins explaining the history of urban zoning; send this overexplanation reaction.
near_miss_context: The listener requested the background and needs it to decide; detail can be relevant rather than excessive.

name: Sofa explosion
message: Use when a calm or comfortable situation is abruptly destroyed by a wildly disruptive event.
relational_pattern: Normality holds for one beat before chaos erupts without warning.
example_context: A quiet family chat suddenly receives fifty messages about an old inheritance dispute, and you compare it to the exploding sofa.
near_miss_context: A planned announcement arrives on schedule and everyone responds calmly; expected change is not a surprise detonation.

name: Now that's a name I haven't heard since...
message: Use when hearing an old name or topic that revives distant memories
relational_pattern: An old reference triggers nostalgic recollections
example_context: A friend mentions an abandoned app everyone used in college, and you answer with the old-name line.
near_miss_context: The subject was discussed yesterday and remains active; the reference is not distant enough to awaken nostalgia.

name: Baby Boss Relaxed Smug Content
message: Use when relaxed smugness follows getting exactly what was wanted
relational_pattern: You feel content after achieving a desired outcome
example_context: Your proposal is approved exactly as written, so you post the relaxed Boss Baby while everyone else debates revisions.
near_miss_context: You are still waiting anxiously for a decision; smug contentment would claim an outcome that has not arrived.

name: I am the danger
message: Use when rejecting the role of victim and claiming to be the real threat
relational_pattern: You assert yourself as the source of danger rather than the target
example_context: A competitor warns that your teammate may be outmatched, and the teammate replies that they are the danger.
near_miss_context: You face a credible threat and are asking others for protection; dominance would be empty bravado.

name: Why would X do this
message: Use when someone causes a problem and then hypocritically blames an innocent person, group, or force for it.
relational_pattern: The perpetrator poses as a confused victim of their own deliberate action.
example_context: A manager cancels testing, ships a broken release, and asks why quality assurance allowed it; the team uses this format privately.
near_miss_context: An investigator traces a failure to its actual external cause; accurate attribution is not self-exonerating blame.

name: Girls whispering
message: Use when sharing private gossip or side commentary about someone nearby
relational_pattern: You discuss someone's private matters in a low voice
example_context: Two friends quietly exchange reactions while the person they are discussing gives a speech nearby; use this for the side commentary.
near_miss_context: The comment is addressed openly to the person and everyone can hear it; secrecy is essential to the whispering setup.

name: magic 8 ball
message: Use when handing an uncertain prediction or decision over to arbitrary, pseudo-mystical chance.
relational_pattern: A yes-or-no question receives random guidance instead of evidence-based judgment.
example_context: Nobody knows whether the client will reply today, so a teammate jokingly asks the Magic 8 Ball.
near_miss_context: The team has reliable data and a defined decision rule; pretending the answer is random would ignore usable evidence.

name: Spongebob - "I Don't Need It" (by Henry-C)
message: Use when trying to resist a temptation while desire visibly intensifies
relational_pattern: You struggle against a growing urge to act
example_context: You keep refusing dessert until someone opens the box beside you, then post the panels as your resolve collapses.
near_miss_context: The offer holds no appeal and declining it is effortless; desire must intensify for the progression to work.

name: I am speed
message: Use when psyching yourself up to act exceptionally fast, often with more confidence than the task warrants.
relational_pattern: A declaration of speed precedes a rushed attempt or quick turnaround.
example_context: You have five minutes to clean before guests arrive and post 'I am speed' before starting.
near_miss_context: The work requires slow verification and you intentionally proceed carefully; speed is not the goal.

name: Arrested Development how much would a banana cost
message: Use when someone reveals wealth or privilege by wildly overestimating the price of an ordinary item.
relational_pattern: Distance from everyday costs produces a confidently absurd guess.
example_context: An executive estimates that a bus ticket costs fifty dollars, and employees respond with the banana quote.
near_miss_context: A shopper checks a fluctuating price because they are budgeting carefully; uncertainty is not privileged detachment.

name: Being/working as xxxxxx is not stressful at all
message: Use when someone insists a role or situation is not stressful while their appearance or surroundings prove the opposite.
relational_pattern: Verbal denial clashes with visible evidence of severe strain.
example_context: The event organizer says planning is relaxing while answering three phones and fixing a leak, so the team posts this.
near_miss_context: Someone reports low stress and is visibly calm with a manageable workload; the contradiction required by the meme is absent.

name: 2/3 wolves laugh
message: Use when two members share a joke while a third is excluded or unimpressed
relational_pattern: Two people laugh together while ignoring a third person
example_context: Two teammates laugh at an inside joke while the new colleague stares blankly, so you label the three wolves.
near_miss_context: All three people understand and enjoy the joke together; nobody occupies the excluded or unimpressed role.

name: Dinkleberg Blank
message: Use when using one familiar scapegoat for every unrelated inconvenience
relational_pattern: You blame a common figure for unrelated issues
example_context: The Wi-Fi fails, it rains, and you lose a sock; blame the same rival for all three with a resentful 'Dinkleberg.'
near_miss_context: Evidence connects a specific person to the one problem being discussed; accurate responsibility is not scapegoating.

name: clown computer
message: Use when someone's online post, search, purchase, or argument makes them look foolish by their own hand.
relational_pattern: Digital activity becomes a self-administered clown costume.
example_context: A friend argues with an obvious parody account for an hour, and the group sends this computer-clown reaction.
near_miss_context: A person is deceived by a sophisticated fraud despite reasonable caution; ridicule would unfairly blame the victim.

name: Drunk Guy Talking To Girl
message: Use when someone delivers a long, passionate monologue to a listener who is visibly disengaged or trapped.
relational_pattern: The speaker's intensity grows while the audience offers no reciprocal interest.
example_context: At a party you explain your keyboard layout for twenty minutes to someone scanning the room for an exit; post this afterward.
near_miss_context: Both people ask questions and enthusiastically trade detailed stories; mutual engagement is not a one-sided ramble.

name: Grandpa Simpson Hat
message: Use when someone arrives, immediately recognizes an unwanted situation, and leaves without engaging.
relational_pattern: Entry and exit collapse into one quick reversal after a single glance.
example_context: You join a call, hear that it is an icebreaker session, and disconnect before anyone notices; send this in the private chat.
near_miss_context: A participant stays to address the problem despite initial discomfort; they did not perform the instant turnaround.

name: Homelander applause
message: Use when receiving approval that feels forced, performative, or unsettling
relational_pattern: The approval is generated by external pressure rather than genuine acceptance
example_context: The boss finishes a threatening speech and everyone claps because nobody wants to be first to stop; post this unsettling applause.
near_miss_context: Colleagues spontaneously celebrate a well-earned achievement; genuine warmth lacks the coercive undertone.

name: Fortune Cookie
message: Use to package a prediction, tiny piece of advice, or suspiciously convenient claim as mock fortune-cookie wisdom.
relational_pattern: Authority through packaging: an ordinary opinion is presented as if fate delivered a concise prophecy.
example_context: A friend predicts the delayed bus will arrive the moment everyone orders a taxi, so you frame the guess as today's fortune.
near_miss_context: Avoid when quoting verified guidance from a qualified source; the joke depends on flimsy prophecy or bite-sized pseudo-wisdom.

name: Angry pingu
message: Use when small frustrations escalate into disproportionate fury
relational_pattern: Minor annoyances trigger an exaggerated emotional response that exceeds the initial problem's significance
example_context: The printer jams once during a quiet afternoon and your friend reacts as if personally betrayed, so you send Angry Pingu.
near_miss_context: A repeated failure has serious consequences and the person voices proportionate concern; not all anger is comic excess.

name: Soldiers hold up society
message: Use to show that overlooked workers, systems, or institutions carry the burden that lets everyone else function normally.
relational_pattern: Visible society rests on a small, strained support layer receiving little recognition.
example_context: During a smooth launch, someone credits the two operations engineers quietly keeping every service alive with this image.
near_miss_context: A celebrated leader receives ample support while contributing little infrastructure; placing them underneath society would invert the burden.

name: For Christmas I Want a Dragon
message: Use when an impossible wish is treated as easier to grant than a supposedly realistic but extraordinarily unlikely request.
relational_pattern: The fallback to fantasy exposes how hopeless the original demand sounds.
example_context: A friend asks for a cheap apartment beside the office, and you reply, 'What color dragon would you like?'
near_miss_context: The practical request is readily available within budget; replacing it with fantasy would not reveal impossibility.

name: thank you for changing my life
message: Use to give dramatically oversized gratitude for a small tip, convenience, recommendation, or kindness.
relational_pattern: A modest benefit is celebrated as a life-altering intervention.
example_context: A coworker shows you a keyboard shortcut that saves two clicks, and you respond, 'Thank you for changing my life.'
near_miss_context: Someone provides life-saving aid during an emergency; sincere major gratitude should not be reduced to a tiny-favor joke.

name: Not stonks
message: Use when a decision or outcome is plainly financially or strategically bad
relational_pattern: The result of a choice has clear negative consequences that are obvious to the decision-maker
example_context: You pay rush shipping that costs more than the item, and the group replies 'not stonks.'
near_miss_context: A costly choice buys a clearly valued benefit after informed comparison; expense alone is not strategic failure.

name: Who the f**k starts a conversation like that I just sat down!
message: Use when someone's opening line is so intense, intimate, hostile, or bizarre that it overwhelms the conversation before it begins.
relational_pattern: A listener who has barely arrived is confronted with an inappropriately extreme first remark.
example_context: You join lunch and a friend immediately asks which family member you would rescue first; answer with this line.
near_miss_context: The conversation develops naturally before reaching a difficult subject; the shock depends on the remark coming first.

name: yo dawg i heard you like
message: Use when nesting a thing inside another version of itself so someone can experience it while experiencing it.
relational_pattern: Recursive duplication turns a preference into an absurd layered construction.
example_context: A coworker embeds a dashboard inside a dashboard and says it lets you monitor dashboards while monitoring dashboards.
near_miss_context: You merely recommend a second unrelated item someone may enjoy; parallel suggestions are not recursive nesting.

name: So anyway I started blasting
message: Use when someone skips deliberation and responds to a problem with immediate, excessive, chaotic action.
relational_pattern: A brief setup jumps straight to an overreaction with no measured intermediate step.
example_context: Asked how they handled one spam email, your friend says they blocked the entire company domain: 'Anyway, I started blasting.'
near_miss_context: A team investigates carefully and applies the smallest effective fix; restraint is the opposite of blasting.

name: Thor is he though
message: Use when challenging a confident claim with dry skepticism
relational_pattern: The response questions the validity of a statement through understated doubt
example_context: Someone declares the new hire a genius before their first day, and you answer with Thor's skeptical 'Is he though?'
near_miss_context: The claim is supported by clear evidence and you have no reason to doubt it; reflexive skepticism adds nothing.

name: Tell me the truth, I'm ready to hear it
message: Use when bracing for an unpleasant fact and asking for blunt honesty
relational_pattern: The request for truth is made in anticipation of negative information
example_context: Before opening the review comments, you ask your teammate to tell you plainly how bad they are.
near_miss_context: You are fishing for reassurance and reject every honest answer; the format claims readiness to accept an unpleasant truth.

name: Quit Having Fun
message: Use to mock a scold who condemns other people's harmless enjoyment because it is unfashionable, unserious, or not to their taste.
relational_pattern: Personal dislike is presented as a moral rule that everyone else must stop having fun.
example_context: Someone writes an essay about why adults should not enjoy a silly game, and fans answer with this comic.
near_miss_context: An activity is harming participants or bystanders; criticism based on real consequences is not joyless gatekeeping.

example_context: A friend disputes one date, and you answer with a sourced twenty-page timeline; the group compares it to Dr. Manhattan.
near_miss_context: You offer one concise fact that resolves a consequential dispute; proportionate evidence is not explosive overkill.

relational_pattern: The reaction shows a person's growing irritation from a monotonous activity.

name: WALLSTARS2 EXACTLY! Ogo WALLSTARS2 EXACTLY!
message: Use WALLSTARS2 EXACTLY! Ogo WALLSTARS2 EXACTLY! when you want to respond with repetition to a moment involving exactness.

example_context: For example, a group chat where someone insists on repeating a phrase exactly to avoid confusion.
near_miss_context: Avoid when someone uses it to mean 'exactly' as a standalone word in a different context.

name: I Understood That Reference
message: Use I Understood That Reference when someone finally recognizes an allusion that everyone else already understood.
relational_pattern: A delayed moment of recognition turns shared knowledge into a small personal victory.
example_context: For example, a coworker mentions an obscure movie quote and you are delighted to recognize it.
near_miss_context: Avoid when someone is confused by the reference or only pretends to understand it.

name: Suspicious Oprah Glare
message: Use Suspicious Oprah Glare when a questionable claim earns immediate, silent distrust instead of a verbal challenge.
relational_pattern: One person makes a dubious move while the observer answers with unmistakable suspicion.
example_context: For example, your sibling claims the missing dessert vanished before they entered the kitchen.
near_miss_context: Avoid when the observer is merely surprised, impressed, or openly confronting the speaker.

name: Nick Cannon Thinking
message: Use Nick Cannon Thinking when new information is interesting enough to deserve a closer, more skeptical look.
relational_pattern: Initial curiosity becomes focused consideration as the listener decides whether an idea has merit.
example_context: For example, a friend describes an unexpectedly clever shortcut that might actually solve your problem.
near_miss_context: Avoid when the reaction is immediate approval, total confusion, or complete disinterest.

name: You Salty?
message: Use You Salty? when teasing someone whose bitterness is obvious after losing an argument or competition.
relational_pattern: A winner playfully calls attention to the loser's exaggerated resentment.
example_context: For example, your friend blames the controller after losing the same game three times.
near_miss_context: Avoid when the frustration is serious, justified, or unrelated to losing status.

name: Everything Hurts and I Am Dying
message: Use Everything Hurts and I Am Dying when ordinary exhaustion feels catastrophically worse than the situation deserves.
relational_pattern: A manageable discomfort is described with theatrical, total physical collapse.
example_context: For example, you finish one workout after months away and every staircase becomes an enemy.
near_miss_context: Avoid when someone faces a genuine medical emergency or calmly reports minor discomfort.

name: How Do You Do, Fellow Kids?
message: Use How Do You Do, Fellow Kids? when someone tries painfully hard to appear younger or culturally current.
relational_pattern: An obvious outsider adopts superficial youth signals while fooling nobody in the group.
example_context: For example, a manager adds three-year-old slang to a mandatory company announcement.
near_miss_context: Avoid when someone naturally belongs to the group or uses current language without forcing it.
